problem: Earlier grounded-language tasks each cover only part of the picture. Visually grounded dialogue (Visual Dialog, GuessWhat) has perception and dialogue but no action. Instruction following (R2R/VNL) has perception and action but no interactive dialogue. Embodied QA uses simulated perception and scripted language. No large dataset combined real perception, navigation actions and two-way human dialogue, and no architecture existed for grounding a communicated trajectory (observations plus actions) onto an overhead map to localize the speaker.
motivation: The authors argue that human language acquisition involves perception, action and interactive communication together, so a task needing all three is needed. In Talk the Walk a guide holds a landmark map and the target but not the tourist's position, and a tourist sees 360° NYC street views. Uncertainty about the tourist's location is what drives the dialogue, which makes tourist localization the key sub-task. A Bayes upper-bound analysis shows one landmark observation localizes only ~35% of the time, while a short trajectory including actions exceeds 90%. So models must ground both observations and actions into the map.
key_idea: Collect a large crowd-sourced guide–tourist navigation dialogue dataset on real 360° NYC street views, and localize the tourist with MASC (Masked Attention for Spatial Convolutions). MASC turns each communicated action into a softmax 3x3 spatial mask on a learned convolution, which translates the guide's landmark-map embedding along the implied state transition before matching it against the communicated observations.
insight: Actions carry most of the localization signal. The Bayes upper bound with observations only plateaus around 57% (T=3 test 55.84), but reaches 92.41 when actions are used. Without MASC the guide cannot exploit actions and stays near 43% (T=3 test: cont 33.11 / disc 43.51). With MASC it reaches 69.85 / 69.51, and in the full task 88.33 vs 43.54 for continuous T=3. Continuous and discrete emergent channels perform similarly, so discreteness does not limit localization. With natural language the bottleneck is language: human utterances localize poorly (16.17 test) because they rarely name the observed landmark. Generated utterances that mention the current landmark do better (29.05, greedy). However, generators cannot describe multi-step trajectories: full-task success falls from 50.00 (T=0) to 22.50 (T=3). Larger beams also hurt (29.05 at beam 1 → 20.87 at beam 8).
method: Talk the Walk environment/dataset: 360° photos at all four corners of intersections in 5 NYC neighborhoods (~10x10 corner grid each), each corner annotated with coarse landmark categories (bar, bank, shop, coffee shop, restaurant, theater, playfield, hotel, subway). Episodes sample a 4x4 sub-grid. The tourist moves with turn-left/turn-right/forward; the guide sees the landmark map and target and can call EVALUATE (3 failed attempts allowed). 10,310 successful MTurk dialogues collected via ParlAI; splits hold out intersections (test: all four intersections novel).

Simplifications for modeling: 'perfect perception' (the tourist observes the ground-truth landmark symbols of its current corner instead of images, because ResNet-152 / text-recognition landmark classifiers barely beat an all-positive baseline) and 'orientation-agnosticism' (actions become Left/Right/Up/Down map moves, implying a compass).

Tourist message generation over three channels: (a) continuous vectors, i.e. sums of positionally-gated landmark and action embeddings; (b) discrete symbols, i.e. Bernoulli samples of the gated embeddings trained with REINFORCE using the negative guide loss as reward plus a learned linear baseline; (c) natural language from an LSTM decoder conditioned on LSTM encodings of observations and actions, trained with teacher forcing and optionally fine-tuned with policy gradient against a frozen guide.

Guide message decoding: linear layers extract per-step action embeddings from emergent messages. For natural language, a BiLSTM with an iterative control-vector attention extracts per-step observation and action embeddings. A softmax-regression head predicts the trajectory length T, trained with REINFORCE.

MASC: each action embedding is projected to 9 logits, softmaxed and reshaped into a 3x3 mask. The mask is broadcast over the feature dimensions of a learned 3x3xNxN kernel (Hadamard product), and the masked convolution is applied to the 4x4 map embedding U_t → U_{t+1}, repeated T times with zero padding.

Location prediction: positionally-gated sum of the T+1 map embeddings, dot product with the observation embedding, and a softmax over the 16 locations. Trained with cross-entropy (Adam) and early stopping on validation accuracy.

Full-task baseline protocol: the tourist does a random walk with a sliding T-step buffer. At each step it messages the guide, which samples a location; if that location equals the target the position is evaluated, and the episode fails after 3 wrong evaluations.

setting.backbone: Small task-specific networks trained from scratch: embedding/LSTM tourist + guide with MASC (masked 3x3 convolutions over a 4x4 landmark-embedding map); BiLSTM-attention guide encoder for natural language
setting.model_size: not reported (small; L=500 embeddings for emergent models, 128-d word embeddings + 256-unit BiLSTM for NL)
setting.training_data: Talk the Walk dataset: 10,310 successful (plus 3,124 failed) crowd-sourced guide–tourist dialogues over 5 NYC neighborhoods, >10K vocabulary, ~62 acts per dialogue. Emergent models are trained on random walks over training grids. NL models are trained on tourist utterances with the observations/actions extracted between utterances from human trajectories; the full-task NL guide also uses random trajectories.
setting.observation: Tourist: under 'perfect perception', the set of ground-truth landmark category symbols at the current corner (the raw task gives planar projections of 360° street-view images). Guide: 4x4 overhead map with landmark categories, no street names.
setting.action_space: Raw task: discrete turn left / turn right / forward on a grid of intersection corners, plus guide EVALUATE_LOCATION. Modeling: orientation-agnostic Left/Right/Up/Down grid moves; the guide outputs a distribution over 16 map locations.
setting.simulator: custom 2D-grid street-view environment built from manually captured 360° photos of NYC (integrated in ParlAI)
setting.privileged: perfect perception (GT landmark labels of the current corner given to the tourist instead of images); compass-aligned orientation-agnostic actions; the guide has the annotated landmark map (part of the task)

Mapping: 'val' = paper's Valid, 'test' = paper's Test. Train accuracies are omitted. The full-task '#steps' column is a single column not tied to a split; it is attached here to the test entries. In the appendix full-task table, the T=2 and T=3 MASC discrete rows are identical (86.23/82.81/87.08/34.83), a likely copy error; 'Best Disc.' reuses these numbers. The full-task random baseline is 18.75 and human success is 76.74 (dataset completion rate, 15.05 steps). Other reported results not listed as entries: appendix ablations (beam size, path length T=0..3, 1/3/5-utterance context with and without MASC) and landmark-classification F1 scores.
results: On the full task, the best localization-based baseline (continuous emergent communication with MASC, T=3) reaches 88.33% test success. This exceeds the 76.74% human rate under the perfect-perception assumption, though it needs ~34 steps vs ~15 for humans. The discrete channel gets 87.08% and the natural-language tourist only 50.00%, vs 18.75% random. MASC roughly doubles emergent localization accuracy over the no-MASC guide (69.85 vs 33.11 test at T=3, continuous), which plateaus near 43%. Natural-language localization is much harder: 16.17% from human utterances (20.33% with 5 utterances of context) and 29.05% from supervised greedy generated utterances.
limitations: Relies on 'perfect perception': the tourist receives ground-truth landmark symbols instead of images, because ResNet/text-recognition landmark classifiers barely beat trivial baselines. Also relies on orientation-agnostic, compass-aligned actions, so the real visual and orientation problem is unsolved.

The full-task baseline is only a localization model plus a random-walk tourist. The guide never generates navigation instructions, the tourist does not follow guidance, and many more steps than humans are needed.

Natural-language models ground only a single landmark observation. Human utterances localize poorly, and generated language cannot describe multi-step trajectories (success falls from 50.00 at T=0 to 22.50 at T=3). Grids are tiny (4x4, 16 locations).
